analysis.one_liner: Phases out the routine feeding of medically important antibiotics to farm animals to slow drug resistance.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the withdrawal of federal approvals for feeding medically important antibiotics to food-producing animals for growth promotion and routine disease prevention, unless manufacturers proved the practice caused no harm from drug-resistant bacteria. It offered payments to help livestock and poultry producers transition, with priority for family-owned and small farms, funded university research on phasing out the practice, and required annual public reporting of antibiotic sales. It died in the Senate committee it was referred to, without any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who may someday need an antibiotic to treat a bacterial infection — the bill's stated aim is preserving the effectiveness of existing antibiotics by cutting the largest source of their overuse. Consumers also benefit from the new annual public reporting of antibiotic sales. Livestock producers who phase out routine antibiotic use would get federal payments to defray transition costs, with family-owned and small farms given priority.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who relies on antibiotics; small family farms

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to withdraw approvals for the nontherapeutic use of medically important antibiotics in food-producing animals within two years, unless the drug maker demonstrates a reasonable certainty of no harm to human health from antibiotic resistance.

Cuts an overuse pathway the bill cites as substantial: it cites an estimate that roughly 70% of antimicrobials used in the U.S. are fed to farm animals for nontherapeutic purposes, typically without a prescription.
Authorizes Agriculture Department payments to livestock and poultry producers that substantially reduce nontherapeutic antibiotic use, with priority given to family-owned and small farms and ranches.
Directs grants to universities for research and demonstration programs on phasing out routine antibiotic use, plus producer education through the extension service.
Requires manufacturers to report annual sales of these drugs by animal and purpose, with the information published for the public.
The bill's findings cite the National Academy of Sciences estimating that eliminating antibiotics as feed additives would cost each American consumer less than $5 to $10 per year.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of animal antibiotics, whose nontherapeutic-use approvals would be withdrawn within two years unless they prove safety, and who would face new annual sales reporting. Large livestock and poultry operations that rely on routine antibiotics to promote growth and compensate for crowded, unsanitary conditions would bear adjustment costs, though the bill offers federal payments to help cover them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Animal drug makers and large livestock operations

drawbacks.text: Producers relying on routine antibiotic use for disease prevention in crowded conditions would face adjustment costs during the two-year phaseout, though the bill authorizes payments to defray them and gives priority to small and family farms.

The bill recognizes that some nonroutine preventive uses of antibiotics in animal agriculture are legitimate, so the line between banned routine use and allowed disease response would fall to the Secretary's determinations, which could be contested.
The cost of the producer assistance payments and university research grants would be borne by federal appropriations, with the bill authorizing 'such sums as are necessary' without a specific limit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's own findings put the cost of acting at roughly $5-10 per consumer per year, offset by an estimated $4-5 billion annual cost of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, and note that the European Union's comparable ban produced no significant harm to animal health, productivity, food safety, or meat prices. The main design costs — transition help for producers and research funding — are targeted to easing the change rather than weakening the public-health purpose. The main honest objection is implementation: separating 'routine' from legitimate preventive use would require difficult case-by-case determinations by the Secretary.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced by Sen. Kennedy on July 25, 2003, with original cosponsors including Sen. Snowe, Sen. Reed, and Sen. Bingaman, and referred the same day to the Senate HELP Committee.
The only subsequent action was a star print ordered on July 30, 2003; the committee held no markup and the bill never reached the Senate floor.
The bill carried five cosponsors at the end of the Congress, four Democrats and one Republican.
The bill's findings cite support from more than 300 organizations including the American Medical Association and the American Public Health Association.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Animal antibiotic manufacturers and large livestock operations that continued routine antibiotic feeding, since the public-health restrictions never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Animal drug makers and large livestock producers

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to measure party lines; the bill drew a small bipartisan group of sponsors (four Democrats and one Republican) and died quietly in committee without recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill would withdraw FDA approvals for nontherapeutic uses of medically important antibiotics within two years unless makers proved no resistance harm, and impose annual public sales reporting. Their existing sales of routine feed additives depended on approvals granted before the FDA weighed resistance, which the bill's findings say covered most antibiotics then used in animal production.

The bill would end their access to routine antibiotics for growth promotion and to compensate for crowded conditions, forcing changes in husbandry, but offers federal payments to defray transition costs. The bill's findings cite EU experience showing no significant impact on animal health, productivity, or meat prices after a comparable ban.

industries.industry: Family-owned and small farms and ranches
industries.note: They would receive priority for transition payments to help reduce routine antibiotic use, easing their adjustment relative to larger operations.
